description: Width tiers for Languages — Background Language Learner Pathway, Years 1–2 band
subject: Languages — Background Language Learner

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term at Y1-2. For communicating descriptors: the minimum range of interaction types, text types or task contexts in which students have demonstrated the capability. For understanding descriptors: the minimum range of language features or cultural contexts noticed and described.
width_notes.typical_width: The full descriptor scope from ACARA elaborations — what a well-taught Y1-2 background language learner class would have engaged with across the breadth of the descriptor.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new task contexts (for communicating descriptors) or new language/cultural phenomena (for understanding descriptors). Background language learners' authentic home-language experience is a key width resource.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations for the Chinese Background Language Learner pathway (Y1-2) used as source data. Chinese-specific references are preserved as representative examples of the generic target-language principle.

AC9LCH2C01.minimum_width: Use appropriate greetings and terms of address for different people and times of day; respond correctly to at least three classroom routine instructions; share at least three pieces of personal information using modelled sentence structures.
AC9LCH2C01.typical_width: Use contextually appropriate greetings and address forms; participate in classroom routine exchanges; share and request personal information in introduction exchanges; use polite requests, thanks, apologies and expressions of preference; use formulaic exclamations spontaneously with peers; create short interactive texts (emails, messages, invitations) using appropriate conventions.
wider: Conduct an extended role-play introduction exchange incorporating personal information sharing and questions, sustaining for at least four turns across different partner types
Compare greeting and politeness conventions in the target language with English and other known languages — identify what changes across contexts and relationships
Use digital communication formats to exchange personal information with a peer, applying appropriate format conventions
elaborations: greeting each other and using appropriate terms of address, gestures, and body language for different times of day and relationships
responding to classroom instructions and routines
sharing personal information about topics such as age, zodiac animal sign, class and school
making simple requests using appropriate manners
using puppets to perform role-play exchanges about family
expressing thanks, apologies, likes and dislikes
using formulaic exclamations spontaneously when interacting with peers
identifying which languages they know and are learning

AC9LCH2C02.minimum_width: Participate actively in at least two songs, rhymes or structured language games demonstrating meaning through action; take a turn leading or directing an activity, giving at least one instruction in the target language.
AC9LCH2C02.typical_width: Participate in songs, rhymes, chants and games with repetitive language and physical actions; take turns giving instructions and leading activities; participate in role-play scenarios using props and costumes; work collaboratively to create labelled shared products; play matching and memory games using target language words.
wider: Design and explain the rules of a simple game using target language instruction forms, then lead a small group through it
Extend a familiar role-play scenario with additional turns or a new episode, introducing a complication and negotiating a resolution
Identify and compare play-based interaction conventions in the target language community with those of other communities represented in the class
elaborations: participating in singing songs, and reciting rhymes and chants that use repetitive language and actions
participating in play-based experiences using props or dress-up costumes
using pictures or prompts to participate in speaking and listening activities with peers
collaborating in games that involve taking turns, making choices or swapping items
playing matching games with target language and English words from big books
taking turns leading games or activities
giving instructions such as taking the role of a physical education teacher
working collaboratively to identify and label objects or places on a word wall or map

AC9LCH2C03.minimum_width: Identify at least three key words from a familiar text and demonstrate understanding of the main point through gesture, image or ordering; express at least one opinion about a character using a modelled sentence structure.
AC9LCH2C03.typical_width: Locate key words and main points in familiar spoken and written texts; make connections between text content and personal experience and world knowledge; identify details about characters and events; express opinions about characters and retell storylines using modelled language; draw and label scenes from texts; recognise that gestures and body language contribute to meaning in communication.
wider: Compare the world of a familiar text (characters, settings, events) with personal experience — discuss what is similar, different or surprising
Compare how information is conveyed across two different text types — spoken story, song, and written text — identifying what each format does differently
Identify examples from First Nations Australian communication contexts where gesture and body language carry meaning, connecting to how this also occurs in the target language
elaborations: making connections between a simple text and self
making connections between world knowledge and target language to infer meaning of words
identifying details about people and events heard, seen or read in media

recognising that gestures and body language are integral to communicating in language for First Nations Australians, and showing examples of how they are also integral to communicating in the target language
showing understanding of main points in spoken and written texts
listening to imaginative texts and responding through play-acting or movement
identifying key words in familiar texts such as stories and rhymes
drawing and labelling a character or scene from rhymes or stories
participating in shared reading and responding to questions
identifying and justifying a favourite character using modelled language
expressing opinions about characters or retelling storylines after viewing or listening

AC9LCH2C04.minimum_width: Identify and use at least two politeness or address conventions in the target language, explaining why each is used; identify at least one culturally-specific expression that cannot be directly translated into English and explain its meaning in context.
AC9LCH2C04.typical_width: Demonstrate levels of politeness in different social contexts; identify and use appropriate address forms for different relationships; understand and apply cultural gesture conventions; identify expressions in the target language that carry specific cultural meaning; compare with English equivalents; interpret non-verbal cues in animations, songs and interaction texts.
wider: Research a culturally-specific occasion or celebration and identify the language specifically associated with it — explain why particular expressions are used on that occasion and not others

Compare non-verbal communication conventions in the target language with gesture and body language in First Nations Australian communication — identify similarities and differences in how gesture carries meaning
Compare politeness conventions in the target language with English — identify where the conventions differ most and what this reveals about cultural values
elaborations: discussing the different implications of direct versus polite request forms
showing politeness in different contexts, making requests with appropriate register
learning about etiquette in everyday social contexts such as how to address adults
understanding cultural gestures, for example, standing up to greet a teacher, receiving an object with both hands
creating bilingual resources such as illustrated word charts or digital flashcards
discussing words or expressions that appear to have no equivalent in English
discussing meanings of colloquial phrases used on specific occasions
interpreting language, facial expressions and other visual cues in animations or songs

AC9LCH2C05.minimum_width: Copy at least five target language words with correct script conventions; create at least one short text (caption, card, poster, or label) using at least three target language words or a modelled phrase for a clear communicative purpose.
AC9LCH2C05.typical_width: Copy and produce written target language with attention to script conventions using varied materials; create a range of short texts — captions, greeting cards, posters, illustrated sentences, self-portraits with labels; combine target language with images and other modes; role-play modelled conversations; perform short plays using puppets and props; present personal knowledge about places and experiences.
wider: Create a bilingual text communicating the same information in both the target language and English — compare the choices made and what is easier or harder to express in each
Create a text for a specific real audience (younger students, family, community) and adapt language choices accordingly
Create and perform an original short play or role-play using known language in a new scenario for a real or realistic audience
elaborations: writing captions with support for a photographic display about a class event
drawing a picture around a component or character depicting the meaning
creating posters on a cultural topic selecting images and texts
matching bilingual captions to images of First Nations Country/Place locations in their local area or elsewhere in Australia
presenting knowledge of places in the target language country and Australia using photographs
role-playing a modelled conversation related to daily life
creating short plays based on extracts from familiar stories using puppets and props
practising language using toys, puppets and dolls
making a birthday card or drawing and labelling a self-portrait

AC9LCH2U01.minimum_width: Correctly identify at least two different tones when heard and demonstrate that a tone change produces a different meaning; write at least three syllables in the target language phonetic system with correct tone marks.
AC9LCH2U01.typical_width: Identify and distinguish the full tonal system including neutral tone; participate in tone-guessing activities and matching games; write syllables with correct tone marks; understand that the phonetic system represents spoken sounds; match phonetic forms to syllables; identify syllables in words; recite familiar rhymes and poems with attention to tone and rhythm.
wider: Record own pronunciation of different tones and compare with a peer or model — identify where tones sound the same or different and discuss
Analyse the tone patterns in a familiar tongue twister or rhyme — identify which tones recur and whether they contribute to the rhythm or musical effect
Investigate the syllable and tonal structure of a familiar text — explain the pattern and how it differs from English prosody
elaborations: listening to and performing nursery rhymes and stories with rhythms, tones and sound patterns
participating in tone-guessing activities identifying the 4 tones and the neutral tone
writing syllables in the phonetic system with correct tone marks
recording own pronunciation of different tones and playing games with peers
singing a Pinyin alphabet song understanding that Pinyin is the romanisation of spoken sounds
playing pair-matching card games matching tones, initial to final
identifying syllables that make up target language words
developing fluency of sentences using gesture to demonstrate tone and stress

AC9LCH2U02.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of how components or elements combine in the target language to build a word or character and explain the connection to meaning; identify the basic subject-verb-object word order and use at least one grammatical feature (adjective, preposition, or question word) in a modelled sentence.
AC9LCH2U02.typical_width: Explore how characters or words are constructed from components or morphemes; make connections between shared components and related meanings; use basic word order; use common adjectives, prepositions, question words and measure words in modelled sentences; notice similarities and differences in punctuation conventions between the target language and English.
wider: Investigate a group of characters or words sharing a common component — identify the semantic or phonetic connection and explain the pattern to a peer
Compare how words are built in the target language with how compound words work in English — identify similarities and differences in word construction logic
Create a set of annotated sentences demonstrating different grammatical features — label each component to show how it contributes to meaning
elaborations: making and copying components, characters and/or words using playdough, strings, found objects, blocks and chalk
copying and tracing words and phrases with attention to stroke order
making connections among characters sharing the same radicals and discussing the importance of the associated meaning
learning that target language words are made up of multiple characters, each contributing meaning
noticing similarities and differences between punctuation conventions in the target language and English
understanding that there are basic rules of word order: subject+verb+object
using common adjectives to describe people, animals and objects in modelled sentences
recognising common prepositions relating to location
using some question words in familiar contexts
using basic measure words in modelled sentences

AC9LCH2U03.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of word order similarity between the target language and English and at least one example of word order difference with a correct explanation; identify at least two borrowed words in the target language and explain what they mean.
AC9LCH2U03.typical_width: Compare word order in statements, questions and phrases across the target language and English; explore borrowed vocabulary in the target language from other languages and English; compare bilingual texts and notice similarities and differences in punctuation, layout and organisation; use simple metalanguage to describe word types across both languages.
wider: Compare bilingual versions of the same text and map all structural differences — annotate a short text to show where target language and English word order matches and where it diverges
Research the history of a set of borrowed words in the target language — trace where they came from and identify patterns in what gets borrowed (food, technology, fashion)
Explore a grammatical category that works differently in the target language from English — explain the difference in simple terms to a peer
elaborations: noticing that simple statements in Chinese tend to follow the same word order as in English: subject+verb+object
discussing the placement of words in Chinese, for example, 'happy' in Happy Birthday versus the target language equivalent
comparing the vowel sounds of English with the main vowel sounds of the target language
identifying the similarities and differences between cardinal and ordinal numbers in the target language and English
comparing bilingual texts noticing similarities and differences in punctuation and text organisation
recognising that languages use words borrowed from other languages
learning metalanguage for word types, for example, what are considered verbs in English and adjectival verbs in the target language

AC9LCH2U04.minimum_width: Identify at least two communities or regions where the target language is spoken and describe at least one way language use differs across them; identify at least two cultural symbols or practices associated with the target language and describe the language used in connection with each.
AC9LCH2U04.typical_width: Compare and contrast classroom interactions with those in target language communities; identify countries and regions where the target language is used; use culturally appropriate gestures and phrases; explore cultural symbols, practices and celebrations through stories, songs, dances and crafts; share information about own family languages and cultural background.
wider: Compare how First Nations Australian languages are each associated with specific communities and places — discuss similarities with how the target language is connected to cultural belonging and community identity
Interview a family member or community member about their language history and share findings with the class — reflecting on how language connects people to place, family and community
Create a personal language map or family language tree showing which languages are spoken in the family and community, where, and in which contexts
elaborations: comparing and contrasting classroom interactions with those in target language communities
using gestures, words and phrases that reflect aspects of target language culture
identifying countries and regions where the target language is used as a language of communication
exploring symbols and language used by First Nations Australians and in target language communities in a range of contexts
discussing the role of the target language in their own lives — cultural events, food preferences, overseas travel
exploring cultural symbols and practices through stories, songs, dances, games and crafts
sharing information about their family — country of origin, languages spoken, current locations of extended family
